Discussion: What fictional character would be your ideal SO, and why?
I'll start: barring the whole dying thing, Cedric Diggory sounded awesome. Hot, smart, kind...the whole package!

Hmmm... that's a tough one.

Conceptually, you're looking for someone who complements you as a person and vice versa, your ideal SO being someone who both challenges and supports you and someone that you can do the same with.

I don't think that's possible for me.

Maybe that's just my low self-esteem talking, but I think ideals are hard to measure up to when we drag our real selves into the picture.

Still, I'll try and bite, getting as close as I can.

Let's see... I'm a writer, a gamer, a rafter, a performer. Raging ego tamed by a huge inferiority complex. I like hot food, rifftrax, and sappy movies. Manga and anime a plus. No country, please. I prefer someone creative and engaging. A second stoic leads to boring conversations. Someone who pushes me to be a better person, but not too hard that I'm extremely uncomfortable.

Looking at movies, books, comics, and games... I wonder.

Maybe... maybe it's cliche. Maybe it's a joke waiting to happen, but... I suppose... Death of the Endless.

Sure, everyone loves her a little, but the more I think about it, she's pretty close to perfect. Knows the value of the self, encourages artists and morose malcontents such as myself (see: her interactions with Dream). Lives life to the fullest at least once every hundred years, but still manages to find joy and sadness in her every day travails. Friendly, but not afraid to call people on their shit (which I sometimes desperately need).

Yeah. I'm going to go with Death of the Endless.

Lectures on differential equations for Feynman integrals

Lectures on differential equations for Feynman integrals

Johannes M Henn [2015 J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. 48 153001]

First posted at https://voat.co/v/Physics/comments/526835

Alt link: https://archive.is/Clcgj

Abstract:

Over the last year significant progress was made in the understanding of the computation of Feynman integrals using differential equations (DE). These lectures give a review of these developments, while not assuming any prior knowledge of the subject. After an introduction to DE for Feynman integrals, we point out how they can be simplified using algorithms available in the mathematical literature. We discuss how this is related to a recent conjecture for a canonical form of the equations. We also discuss a complementary approach that is based on properties of the space–time loop integrands, and explain how the ideas of leading singularities and d-log representations can be used to find an optimal basis for the DE. Finally, as an application of these ideas we show how single-scale integrals can be bootstrapped using the Drinfeld associator of a DE.
